questions.question: Claude asks permission to run a command you don’t understand. What do you do?

options.text: I answer No and ask what the command does
options.explanation: Correct. Only approve once you know what you’re approving.
Claude is usually right, but you’re responsible for your computer. Read and ask.

options.text: I choose “don’t ask again” so I don’t have to read
options.explanation: Then similar commands will be run without asking from now on. Only choose it for actions you understand.

questions.question: Claude needs access to GitHub. What do you do?

options.text: I type my GitHub password into the conversation
options.explanation: Never type passwords into the conversation.

options.text: I sign in myself with the gh tool in the browser
options.explanation: Exactly. Signing in is done in the browser, and the password stays with you.
Don’t use other people’s credentials. Sign in with your own account.

questions.question: Where does an API key belong?

options.text: Directly in the code, so it’s easy to find
options.explanation: The code goes to GitHub, and then the key becomes public.

options.text: In a .env file that has been added to .gitignore
options.explanation: Correct. That way the key stays on your own computer and doesn’t end up on GitHub.

options.text: In the README file, so others can use it too
options.explanation: An API key is like a password: it isn’t shared.
